alt="Expand/Collapse All button" style="max-width:100%;"> Thoughts, tool outputs and code blocks are rendered as collapsible panes so a long assistant response stays readable. Instead of opening or closing them one by one, use the **Expand/Collapse All** toolbar button to toggle every block in the chat at once. The button icon and tooltip switch between *Expand All* and *Collapse All* so you always know what the next click will do. It's handy right after streaming finishes — collapse everything to see the final summary, or expand everything to inspect every tool result. > [[Thinking and Tool Responses]] > [[Keyboard Shortcuts]] > [[Filtering Chat Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Keyboard Shortcuts Dialog</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> Click the keyboard icon in the assistant panel header to open the **Keyboard Shortcuts** dialog. It lists every shortcut the plugin supports, grouped by section — Navigation &amp; Assistant, Session Management, Chat Input, Editing and Stash Diff — with the keys rendered as keyboard badges. Type in the filter field at the top to search by key or action name. Shortcuts that are not currently assigned are collapsed into a single clickable *Unassigned* summary row per section; click it to expand the full list. Press <code>Escape</code> to close the dialog. > [[Keyboard Shortcuts]] > [[Customising the Toolbar]] > [[Input Area Keys]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Global Configuration Setup</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> The first time you start the IDE (and on server restarts), if you are using OpenCode as the harness, the plugin checks for a global OpenCode configuration file at `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (or `opencode.jsonc`). This file holds security settings like file-permission rules and which commands require your approval. If the file is missing, empty, or contains only the `$schema` reference, the chat panel shows a prompt offering to write a starter configuration: * **Set up starter config** — writes the bundled starter file (see [[Configuration Template]]) to your config directory. * **Not now** — defers the prompt for the current IDE session. It won't ask again until you restart the IDE. If an existing file can't be parsed, the prompt instead asks whether to **Replace** it (which overwrites the broken file) or **Keep** it unchanged. Files that already contain real configuration are never touched. When a config prompt was shown, a confirmation hint with an **OK** button appears before the server starts — click it to proceed. The hint also points you to `opencode auth login` and the free models at **Opencode Zen** (https://opencode.ai/docs/zen/) if you haven't added a model provider yet. > [[Configuration Template]] > [[Manage OpenCode Config in NetBeans]] > [[Choose Your Coding Harness]] > [[Post Install]] > [[Restarting the server]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Task Repositories</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> BeanBot integrates with the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard to let you manage tasks alongside your code. Each <b>task repository</b> maps to a plain todo.txt file on disk — readable and editable with any standard todo.txt tool (see the <a href="https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt" target="_blank">todo.txt spec</a>). To get started, create a repository — see [[Creating a Task Repository]]. Once registered, your tasks appear in the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard — see [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]]. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Multiple repositories</div> You can register multiple repositories (e.g. one per project). When adding a task via the AI, specify the repository by name; if only one exists it is used automatically. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Repository name</div> The task repository appears as <b>BeanBot</b> in the NetBeans bugtracking UI (the "Report a New Task" page). This is the connector display name — distinct from the repository's display name, which you set when creating it. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Adding tasks with the AI</div> You can also create tasks conversationally by asking BeanBot to add a task — it uses the built-in <code>add&#95;task</code> MCP tool. See [[Adding Tasks via AI]] for details. > [[Creating a Task Repository]] > [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]] > [[Todo.txt Format]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Todo.txt Format</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> BeanBot stores tasks as plain todo.txt files — one task per line (see the <a href="https://github.com/todotxt/todo.txt" target="_blank">todo.txt spec</a>). The format extends the spec with a small set of BeanBot-specific tokens. Because it's plain text, you can edit your tasks with any todo.txt tool, a text editor, or version control. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Line layout</div> <pre>x (B) 2026-08-02 2026-08-01 Fix the bug @urgent @bug +myproject due:2026-09-01 id:t-1a2b3c4d estimate:5 consumed:2 upd:2026-08-02T10:00:00Z</pre> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Token</th><th>Meaning</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>x </code> (optional prefix)</td><td>Marks the task <b>closed</b>. Its absence means <b>open</b> — there is no <code>status:</code> token.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>(A)</code>–<code>(Z)</code></td><td>Priority letter. Placed immediately after <code>x </code> (or as the first token when open). Native todo.txt syntax.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>YYYY-MM-DD</code> (first date)</td><td>Completion date — only present when the task is closed (<code>x </code>).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>YYYY-MM-DD</code> (second date)</td><td>Creation date — present for both open and closed tasks.</td></tr> <tr><td><i>free text</i></td><td>The task summary. Preserved verbatim on save.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>@word</code></td><td>A <b>tag</b> (e.g. <code>@urgent</code>).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>+word</code></td><td>A <b>project</b> (e.g. <code>+myproject</code>).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>due:YYYY-MM-DD</code></td><td>Due date — a standard todo.txt extension.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>id:t-XXXXXXXX</code></td><td>Stable task id. If missing, BeanBot generates one in NetBeans format.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>estimate:&lt;int&gt;</code></td><td>Estimated effort in arbitrary user-inferred units.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>consumed:&lt;int&gt;</code></td><td>Consumed effort in the same units.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>upd:&lt;iso&gt;</code></td><td>Last-modified timestamp (full ISO-8601).</td></tr> </tbody> </table> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Priority letters</div> BeanBot uses the full A–Z range for priority. In the task editor, priorities are shown as NATO phonetic words (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie … Zulu) but stored as single uppercase letters. A is the highest priority; N (November) is the default. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Tags and projects</div> Tags and projects are stored <b>only</b> as <code>@</code> and <code>+</code> tokens — there is no redundant <code>tags:</code> or <code>projects:</code> mirror. This ensures a load→save round-trip never duplicates them. Tags appear in the dashboard's tag filter; projects are a separate dimension for grouping. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Estimate and consumed</div> <code>estimate</code> and <code>consumed</code> are integers representing <b>arbitrary, user-defined units</b> — BeanBot does not assign them meaning. They are for personal tracking only (e.g. story points, hours, t-shirt sizes). <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">External tool compatibility</div> Unknown tokens are tolerated on read and ignored, so files edited by other todo.txt tools remain compatible. Lines without a parseable task (e.g. blank lines) are skipped. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Reserialization safety</div> When BeanBot reads a task file and writes it back, it preserves: <ul> <li>The summary text byte-for-byte (no reformatting).</li> <li>All <code>@</code>/<code>+</code> tokens exactly as read.</li> <li>All <code>key:value</code> tokens (id, estimate, consumed, upd, due).</li> <li>The positional dates and priority letter.</li> </ul> This means external edits survive a BeanBot save without spurious diffs. > [[Task Repositories]] > gAAQPGEEQAAUDxhBAAAFE8YAQAAxRNGAABA8YQRAABQPGEEAAAUTxgBAADFE0YAAEDxhBEAAFA8YQQAABRPGAEAAMUTRgAAQPGEEQAAUDxhBAAAFE8YAQAAxRNGAABA8YQRAABQPGEEAAAUTxgBAADFE0YAAEDxhBEAAFA8YQQAABRPGAEAAMUTRgAAQPGEEQAAUDxhBAAAFE8YAQAAxRNGAABA8YQRAABQPGEEAAAUTxgBAADFE0YAAEDxhBEAAFA8YQQAABRPGAEAAMUTRgAAQPGEEQAAUDxhBAAAFE8YAQAAxRNGAABA8YQRAABQPGEEAAAUTxgBAADFE0YAAEDxhBEAAFA8YQQAABRPGAEAAMUTRgAAQPGEEQAAUDxhBAAAFE8YAQAAxRNGAABA8YQRAABQPGEEAAAUTxgBAADFE0YAAEDxhBEAAFA8YQQAABRPGAEAAMUTRgAAQPH+P+RtrQIvDl+8AAAAAElFTkSuQmCC" alt="Task Editor" style="max-width:100%;"> The task editor opens when you create or edit a task from the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard or via the assistant toolbar. It has two sections separated by a divider. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Top section — Summary, Tags, Projects</div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><b>Summary*</b></td><td>The task title (required). Shows a grey placeholder ("Enter summary") when empty.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Tags</b></td><td>Chip-based editor for <code>@</code>-prefixed tags. Type a tag and press Enter, or pick from the dropdown. Predefined: bug, documentation, duplicate, enhancement, feedback, home, invalid, wontfix, work.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Projects</b></td><td>Chip-based editor for <code>+</code>-prefixed projects. The dropdown is pre-populated with your currently open NetBeans project names (spaces replaced with hyphens).</td></tr> </tbody> </table> Tags and projects are shown as removable pills. Click the <b>x</b> on a pill to remove it. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Bottom section — Status, Priority, Estimate, Consumed</div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Field</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><b>Status</b></td><td>Open or closed. Defaults to open.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Priority</b></td><td>A–Z letter, shown as NATO phonetic words (Alpha, Bravo, Charlie … Zulu). November (N) is the default.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Estimate</b></td><td>Arbitrary effort units (integer). Defaults to 0.</td></tr> <tr><td><b>Consumed</b></td><td>Arbitrary effort units consumed so far (integer). Defaults to 0.</td></tr> </tbody> </table> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Due dates</div> Due dates are managed via the dashboard's native <b>Schedule</b> submenu (right-click a task &gt; Schedule), not through the task editor. The editor preserves any existing due date rather than exposing one. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Saving</div> The editor uses the bugtracking framework's standard save mechanism — changes are saved when you close the editor and confirm, or when the framework auto-saves. There is no explicit Save button in the form. > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]] > [[Todo.txt Format]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Adding Tasks via AI</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> You can create tasks conversationally by asking BeanBot to add one. The assistant uses the built-in <code>add&#95;task</code> MCP tool to write directly to your task repository. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.4em; margin-bottom: 0;">Example prompts</div> <ul style="margin-top: 0; margin-bottom: 0.2em;"> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Add a task to fix the login bug"</i></li> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Create a high-priority task: refactor the database layer"</i></li> <li><i>"Track a task: write unit tests for the parser, estimate 3 points"</i></li> </ul> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">What you can specify</div> <table class="ug-table"> <thead><tr><th>Parameter</th><th>Description</th></tr></thead> <tbody> <tr><td><code>summary</code></td><td>The task title (required).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>status</code></td><td><code>open</code> or <code>closed</code>. Defaults to open.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>priority</code></td><td>A single uppercase letter A–Z.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>tags</code></td><td>Comma-separated tags (stored as <code>@tag</code> in the file).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>projects</code></td><td>Comma-separated project names (stored as <code>+project</code> in the file).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>dueDate</code></td><td>ISO-8601 date string.</td></tr> <tr><td><code>estimate</code></td><td>Integer (arbitrary effort units).</td></tr> <tr><td><code>consumed</code></td><td>Integer (effort consumed so far).</td></tr> </tbody> </table> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Repository selection</div> If you have multiple task repositories, specify which one to add to: <ul> <li><i>"Add a task to the Backend repo: fix the cache invalidation"</i></li> <li><i>"In the Frontend project, create a task to update the login form"</i></li> </ul> If only one repository exists, it is used automatically. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0;">Updating, closing, and finding tasks</div> <ul style="margin-top: 0; margin-bottom: 0.2em;"> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Rename task t-3 to fix the cache"</i> — <code>update&#95;task</code></li> <li style="margin-bottom: 0.2em;"><i>"Mark the login-bug task as done"</i> — <code>close&#95;task</code></li> <li><i>"Which open tasks mention login?"</i> — <code>search&#95;task</code> (open tasks only, up to 10 matches)</li> </ul> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">How it works</div> The <code>add&#95;task</code> tool creates a new task in the repository's in-memory cache, persists it to the `todo.txt` file (in a background thread), and returns the task id. <code>update&#95;task</code> and <code>close&#95;task</code> change an existing row the same way. The task then appears in the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard immediately. > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Task Editor]] > [[Todo.txt Format]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Creating a Task Repository</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> Each BeanBot task repository maps to a plain todo.txt file on disk. Creating one takes a few clicks: <ol> <li>Go to <b>Tools &gt; Options &gt; Miscellaneous &gt; Tasks</b> (the BeanBot Tasks options panel).</li> <li>Click <b>Add</b> and fill in: <ul> <li><b>Display name</b> — a human-readable label (defaults to your current project name).</li> <li><b>Tasks file</b> — the path to the <code>.txt</code> file. Defaults to <code>beanbot&#95;todo.txt</code> in the project root.</li> </ul></li> <li>Click <b>OK</b>. The repository is registered and its file is loaded (or created if it doesn't exist yet).</li> </ol> You can register multiple repositories (e.g. one per project). Each repository is remembered across IDE restarts; the underlying todo.txt file is user-maintained and never moved by the plugin. Once created, your tasks appear in the NetBeans Tasks Dashboard — see [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]]. > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Using the Tasks Dashboard]] > [[Todo.txt Format]]<div style="display: alt="Using the Tasks Dashboard" style="max-width:100%;"> Once a repository is registered, your tasks appear in the NetBeans <b>Tasks Dashboard</b> (Window &gt; Tasks). You can: <ul> <li><b>Create tasks</b> via the dashboard's "New Task" button or from the assistant's toolbar.</li> <li><b>Edit tasks</b> by double-clicking them — the task editor opens with Summary, Status, Priority, Tags, Projects, Estimate, and Consumed fields. See [[Task Editor]].</li> <li><b>Set due dates</b> via the dashboard's Schedule submenu (right-click a task &gt; Schedule).</li> <li><b>Filter by tags</b> using the Find Tasks query dialog.</li> </ul> The dashboard's Open / Finished grouping follows the task status: tasks marked closed (the todo.txt <code>x </code> prefix) appear under Finished; everything else is Open. Tasks can also be created conversationally via the AI — see [[Adding Tasks via AI]]. > [[Task Repositories]] > [[Task Editor]] > [[Adding Tasks via AI]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Queuing Messages</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> On agents that drop an in-flight prompt if you send another (see below), you don't have to wait for the assistant to finish before typing. While the agent is working (Go/Stop button shows the running state), anything you send is <b>queued</b> instead of interrupting the current turn. When the turn ends, all queued messages are combined into a single prompt and sent automatically. The queue button appears on the toolbar with a small wobble animation while messages are waiting: <ul> <li><b>Send Now</b> — open the queue button's popup menu to flush the queued messages immediately, without waiting for the turn to end.</li> <li><b>Cancel Queue</b> — discard all queued messages.</li> </ul> Queueing is used when a second <code>session/prompt</code> would drop the in-flight turn. That is currently [[Goose Agent]], [[PI Agent]], [[Hermes Agent]], [[Oh My Pi Agent]], and [[OpenClaw Agent]]. Interleaved agents ([[OpenCode]], [[Cursor Agent]], [[Claude Agent]], [[Gemini Agent]]) send immediately instead. If you close or switch sessions before the turn ends, pending messages are cancelled with the rest of the panel state. > [[Chat Features]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Auto-Backup on Turn Start]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">PI Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <a href="https://pi.dev" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Pi</a> is a minimal, extensible **agent harness** — an open-source coding agent CLI built around a unified multi-provider LLM API, an agent runtime with tool calling, and a self-extensible extension system. It deliberately ships no built-in permission system: it runs with the permissions of the user who launched it, so sandbox or containerize it yourself if you need stronger boundaries. To use Pi with BeanBot, install the harness, then the ACP adapter: #### Install Install the harness first (Node.js 22+): <pre><code>npm install -g @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent</code></pre> BeanBot drives Pi through the <code>@geohar/pi-acp</code> adapter — a fork of <code>svkozak/pi-acp</code> that adds the subagent bridge, MCP handling, and multi-root workspaces. It needs <code>pi</code> 0.80.4+ on your <code>PATH</code>: <pre><code>npm install -g @geohar/pi-acp</code></pre> Loading it into Pi as an extension as well is optional — it surfaces the pi-subagents fleet as tasks in the chat: <pre><code>pi install npm:@geohar/pi-acp</code></pre> The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>pi-acp</code> (the adapter, not <code>pi</code> itself). When the session starts, Pi posts a startup banner with its version, context files and extensions, which the plugin renders as a compact info card. The plugin's [[MCP Tools]] reach Pi over ACP: BeanBot passes its MCP server in the session create/load request, and <code>@geohar/pi-acp</code> forwards it to Pi. One setup step remains: - **MCP adapter** — install <a href="https://github.com/nicobailon/pi-mcp-adapter" target="_blank" rel="noopener">pi-mcp-adapter</a> in your Pi packages. The adapter translates the ACP session's servers into a session-scoped config that it hands to Pi via <code>--mcp-config</code>; without it the servers are not loaded and Pi prints a startup notice. No manual <code>mcp.json</code> entry and no fixed port are needed — the server URL is delivered per session. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Goose Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <a href="https://goose-docs.ai/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Goose</a> is an open-source, general-purpose **AI agent harness** from the Agentic AI Foundation (Linux Foundation). It ships as a native desktop app, a CLI, and an embeddable API — all built in Rust — and works with 15+ LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Bedrock, …). Goose speaks the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a> natively, and connects to 70+ extensions via the <a href="https://modelcontextprotocol.io/" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Model Context Protocol</a>. Install the CLI, then configure <code>goose</code> as the Harness in Options (Assistant > Assistant Service) — make sure the binary is on your <code>PATH</code> or specify the full path. What works with Goose in BeanBot: - **[[Queuing Messages]]** — while Goose is working, your messages are queued and combined into one prompt at turn end (Goose, Pi, Hermes, and Oh My Pi all need this; interleaved agents send immediately). - **[[MCP Tools]]** — the plugin hands Goose a token-protected MCP server URL; the AI can read files, navigate the editor, and run git or Mercurial commands from the conversation. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Queuing Messages]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Hermes Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Install</div> - **macOS / Linux**: <pre><code>curl -fsSL https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.sh | bash</code></pre> - **Windows**: <pre><code>irm https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com/install.ps1 | iex</code></pre> After installing, enable ACP support: <pre><code>cd ~/.hermes/hermes-agent uv pip install -e '.&#91;acp&#93;'</code></pre> Requires Python 3.10+. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">About</div> <a href="https://hermes-agent.nousresearch.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Hermes</a> is an open-source **AI agent harness** from Nous Research. It is a Python-based coding agent with built-in tool calling, multi-provider LLM support, and a self-extensible plugin system. Hermes speaks the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a> natively, which is what BeanBot uses to drive it. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>hermes</code>. When the session starts, Hermes reports its available models and modes as structured fields — the plugin uses these to populate the Model and Mode dropdowns automatically. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">OpenCode</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <a href="https://opencode.ai" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OpenCode</a> is an open-source AI coding agent and the default harness for BeanBot. It supports 15+ LLM providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Ollama, OpenRouter, Bedrock, …) and speaks the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a> natively. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">macOS / Linux</div> <pre><code>curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash</code></pre> Or via package managers: - **npm**: <pre><code>npm install -g opencode-ai</code></pre> - **Homebrew**: <pre><code>brew install anomalyco/tap/opencode</code></pre> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Windows</div> On Windows, you can run OpenCode inside **WSL (Windows Subsystem for Linux)**, or use a package manager. To launch OpenCode through WSL from the plugin, enable **Launch through WSL** under `Tools > Options > Assistant > Assistant Service`. The plugin detects `wsl.exe` on your PATH and wraps all OpenCode invocations through WSL automatically, translating your Windows executable path to its WSL mount location. <pre><code>curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash</code></pre> Or via package managers: - **Chocolatey**: <pre><code>choco install opencode</code></pre> - **Scoop**: <pre><code>scoop install opencode</code></pre> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Configuration</div> After installing, create the configuration file: <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">macOS / Linux</div> The config directory is at `$HOME/.config/opencode/`. <pre><code>mkdir -p &#36;HOME/.config/opencode</code></pre> Create `$HOME/.config/opencode/opencode.json` with the starter configuration: <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Windows</div> <pre><code> mkdir "%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode" cd "%USERPROFILE%\.config\opencode" </code></pre> Open Notepad and paste in the starter configuration: > [[Configuration Template]] <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Verify</div> Run this to confirm the configuration is valid: <pre><code>opencode models</code></pre> Then proceed to [[Post Install]] to configure the plugin in NetBeans. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Options Panel Reference]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Pick Your Harness</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> BeanBot doesn't directly talk to AI services, it communicates via coding agents or harnesses, these applications directly interface with LLM providers like Anthropic or OpenAI, and provide authentication, persistence and context management. Most of them support a protocol called ACP or Agent Client Protocol that simplifies and standardises LLM access for IDEs and Editors. BeanBot takes advantage of this capability, we can connect to any provider or model as long as we find a suitable harness that speaks ACP. In this guide you might also see a harness referred to as an ACP Server, an Agent Server, or simply server, in the context of this plugin it's just a conduit for communicating with a remote LLM. These are the harnesses currently supported, pick the one you want to use. Even unlisted ones might work, but you have to experiment and find out. > [[OpenCode]] > [[PI Agent]] > [[Goose Agent]] > [[Claude Agent]] > [[Cursor Agent]] > [[Hermes Agent]] > [[Gemini Agent]] > [[Oh My Pi Agent]] > [[OpenClaw Agent]] If you are not sure, The plugin will detect installed harnesses and let you choose at startup — see [[Choose Your Coding Harness]]. > [[Home]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Claude Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">Install</div> All platforms (requires Node.js 18+): <pre><code>npm install -g @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp</code></pre> The package bundles the Claude Agent SDK, so a separate `claude` CLI install is not needed. <div style="font-weight: bold; margin-top: 0.8em; margin-bottom: 0.2em;">About</div> <a href="https://github.com/agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Claude Agent ACP</a> is an ACP adapter that exposes Claude's coding agent over the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a>, which is what BeanBot speaks. It supports session mode switching, MCP server injection, and editor context. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>claude-agent-acp</code>. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Cursor Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> #### Install - **macOS / Linux**: `curl https://cursor.com/install -fsSL | bash` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `irm 'https://cursor.com/install?win32=true' | iex` Register once with the CLI (`agent login`, or set `CURSOR_API_KEY`) before connecting. #### About <a href="https://cursor.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Cursor</a> is an AI-powered code editor with a built-in coding agent. Its CLI exposes an ACP entry point that BeanBot can drive. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>cursor-agent</code>. The ACP entry point is the CLI itself, run with `agent acp`. Cursor sends MCP server config and editor context automatically. Cursor is **interleaved**: you can send another message while a turn is still running. The new prompt is issued immediately (it is not held in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue). The previous request finishes as cancelled; the input stays busy until the latest prompt completes. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Gemini Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> #### About <a href="https://geminicli.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Gemini CLI</a> is an AI agent command-line tool. It natively supports communication with external tools using the <a href="https://agentclientprotocol.com" target="_blank" rel="noopener">Agent Client Protocol</a>. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>gemini</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>--acp --model gemini-3.5-flash</code>. When you pick Gemini in the harness chooser or Options, BeanBot reminds you to change <code>--model</code> in Process Arguments if you want a different model. Gemini Agent in BeanBot supports: - **Editor Context**: Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **MCP Servers**: Automatically registers and injects the plug-in's [[MCP Tools]]. - **Client-Side Session Tracking**: Gemini CLI does not publish a session list, so BeanBot keeps session IDs on this machine. Sessions whose project is closed are hidden from the dropdown until that project is open again; IDs are kept so the chat can return. [[Archiving Sessions]] is local only. - **Interleaved prompts**: a new message is sent immediately (it does not wait in the [[Queuing Messages]] toolbar queue). See [[Cursor Agent]] for the same style. #### Model Selection Since Gemini CLI does not support changing the model dynamically via <code>session/set&#95;config&#95;option</code> once the session has started, you can configure your preferred model in one of three ways: 1. **Launch Arguments**: In the plugin options (<code>Tools > Options > Assistant</code>, Process Arguments), set e.g. <code>--acp --model gemini-2.5-pro</code>. 2. **Settings File**: Define the default model in your global configuration file at <code>~/.gemini/settings.json</code>. 3. **Environment Variable**: Set the <code>GEMINI&#95;MODEL</code> environment variable before launching NetBeans. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Choose Your Coding Harness]] > [[Options Panel Reference]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Archiving Sessions]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">Oh My Pi Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> #### Install - **macOS / Linux**: `curl -fsSL https://omp.sh/install | sh` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `irm https://omp.sh/install.ps1 | iex` - **Homebrew**: `brew install can1357/tap/omp` Then run <code>omp</code> in a terminal and use <code>/login</code> to authenticate a model provider. ACP docs: <a href="https://omp.sh/docs/acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">omp.sh/docs/acp</a>. #### About **Oh My Pi (omp)** is an open-source, terminal-based AI coding agent forked from the Pi agent, designed to be a "batteries-included" version integrating full IDE-like capabilities into a terminal harness. Source: <a href="https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi" target="_blank" rel="noopener">can1357/oh-my-pi</a>. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>omp</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>acp</code>. Oh My Pi Agent in BeanBot supports: - **Editor Context**: Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **MCP Servers**: Automatically registers and injects the plug-in's [[MCP Tools]]. - **[[Queuing Messages]]**: Queues and batches user prompts at turn end. - **Session Management**: Supports full session lists and state persistence. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Choose Your Coding Harness]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]]<div style="display: flex; justify-content: space-between; align-items: center; margin-bottom: 1rem;"> <div style="font-weight: bold; text-align: left; flex-grow: 1;">OpenClaw Agent</div> <div>[[Index->Topic Index]]</div> </div> <i style="opacity: 0.7;">Experimental — BeanBot's support for this harness is under active development and may change without notice.</i> #### Install - **macOS / Linux**: `curl -fsSL https://openclaw.ai/install.sh | bash` - **Windows (PowerShell)**: `iwr -useb https://openclaw.ai/install.ps1 | iex` Requires **Node 24.16+ or 26.1+** — Node 26 is recommended, and the installer provisions Node when it is missing. ACP docs: <a href="https://docs.openclaw.ai/cli/acp" target="_blank" rel="noopener">docs.openclaw.ai/cli/acp</a>. #### About <a href="https://docs.openclaw.ai" target="_blank" rel="noopener">OpenClaw</a> is a personal AI assistant gateway. Running <code>openclaw acp</code> makes it act as an **ACP server**: the bridge speaks ACP over stdio, forwards each prompt to an OpenClaw **Gateway** over WebSocket, and maps each ACP session onto a Gateway session key. A running Gateway (local or remote) is required — the bridge routes work into it rather than hosting the agent itself. The executable you configure in BeanBot is <code>openclaw</code>, run with the default launch argument <code>acp</code>. OpenClaw Agent in BeanBot supports: - **Editor Context**: Seamlessly injects the active editor state into agent prompts. - **[[Permission Requests]]**: Gateway exec-approval prompts during a turn are relayed into BeanBot's permission UI. - **Thinking Responses**: Model thinking streams into the chat as thought bubbles. - **[[Queuing Messages]]**: Queues and batches user prompts at turn end. - **Client-Side Session Tracking**: OpenClaw's ACP bridge accepts session-list requests but returns an empty list, so BeanBot keeps session IDs on this machine instead. Sessions whose project is closed are hidden from the dropdown until that project is open again; IDs are kept so the chat can return. [[Archiving Sessions]] is local only. #### Limitations OpenClaw runs as a **bridge** rather than a full ACP-native runtime, so a few ACP surfaces are unavailable: - **MCP Servers**: The bridge rejects per-session MCP servers, so BeanBot cannot hand OpenClaw the plugin's [[MCP Tools]] automatically — it sends no server list. OpenClaw still supports MCP: run the plugin's internal server on a fixed port (**Internal MCP Server** and **Internal MCP Server Port** under <code>Options &gt; Assistant &gt; System</code>) and register that URL as a Gateway MCP server with <code>openclaw mcp add</code> (or <code>mcp.servers</code> in the OpenClaw config, or the Control UI's <code>/settings/mcp</code> page). The Gateway must run on the same machine, because the plugin's server binds to <code>127.0.0.1</code>. - **Model Selection**: Not exposed as an ACP config option, so the in-session model dropdown is unavailable. Change the model from within the chat with <code>/acp set model provider/model</code> — for example <code>/acp set model opencode-go/glm-5.3-flash</code>. - **Agent / Mode Dropdown**: OpenClaw routes by Gateway session key rather than advertising an agent list, so BeanBot does not offer the agent selector. To target a specific agent, add <code>--session agent:&lt;id&gt;:main</code> under Process Arguments in <code>Options &gt; Assistant</code>. > [[Post Install]] > [[Starting a Session]] > [[Choose Your Coding Harness]] > [[MCP Tools]] > [[Permission Requests]] > [[Picking an Agent, Model and Thinking Level]] > [[Queuing Messages]] > [[Archiving Sessions]]
